title: Infra GPU Fleet: Capacity, Cloud Accounts, Networking, Terraform/IaC & CI/CD Runbook
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary:

This runbook consolidates Redwood Inference’s operational guidance for the GPU fleet and related infrastructure: capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking requirements, Terraform/IaC module patterns, CI/CD build and deployment pipelines, and common runbook procedures for scaling, maintenance and incident response. It is intended for infra engineers, SRE, and platform owners responsible for provisioning and operating GPU-backed inference clusters.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Provide a single reference that reduces time-to-action during capacity changes and incidents, enforces standard IaC patterns, and documents safe procedures for scaling and maintenance.
- Scope: Public cloud GPU fleets (primary: AWS, secondary: GCP), tenant cloud accounts and VPC/networking, Terraform modules and repo layout, CI/CD pipelines for infra changes, pre-approved runbook actions for operational events. This doc does NOT cover model-serving runtime internals (see eng-serving-runtime).

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owner: Infra Engineering (oncall rotation)
- Fleet product owner: Platform team
- Pager escalation: infra-oncall -> infra-2 -> platform-eng-lead -> CTO
- Contacts: 
  - Infra lead: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.ai)
  - Capacity planner: Arjun Patel (arjun@redwood.ai)
  - Networking: Lucía González (lucia@redwood.ai)

Key SLA / SLO targets relevant to capacity planning:
- Control plane API latency: P99 < 200ms (when healthy)
- Provisioning time for new GPU nodes (automation): target < 30 min from apply -> ready
- Capacity buffer: maintain 15% available GPU slots for burst workloads (adjust quarterly)
- Autoscale convergence time (add/remove): target 5 minutes

GPU fleet inventory (reference):
| GPU family | Typical instance types (AWS) | Use cases | Notes |
|------------|----------------------------|----------|-------|
| A10 / A10G | g5 / g5n | Batch/medium throughput models | Cost-efficient, good mixed workloads |
| A100      | p4d / p4| High-throughput production, large models | Preferred for Dedicated pools |
| H100      | p5 | Highest perf for 8k+ seq and large Qs | Limited regional availability |
| T4        | g4dn | Small-scale dev and inference | Used in dev pools and CI |

Capacity planning workflows:
1. Weekly capacity review: capacity planner runs usage dashboard, forecasts next 30/90 days, updates PR for capacity changes.
2. Monthly quota review: check cloud account quotas (GPUs, ENIs, EBS IOPS), request increases 2-4 weeks ahead.
3. Pre-scheduled events: for major launches or benchmarks, file an "event capacity" request with required GPU-hours and desired region distribution.

Cloud accounts & networking requirements:
- Account structure: one production account per cloud region (primary), one staging account per region, and a shared infra tooling account.
- VPC design: dedicated VPC per account with public/private subnets; GPU nodes in private subnets with NAT gateways and interface endpoints for S3/KMS.
- Security: host-based SGs lock to control plane IPs, node-to-node mTLS mandatory, KMS for disk encryption.
- Cross-account access: use IAM roles with short-lived STS credentials; Terraform assumes role in target account via CI/CD.

Terraform / IaC standards and repo layout:
- Repo structure (recommended):
  - infra-root/ (global CI configs)
  - modules/ (reusable modules: vpc, compute/gpu-node-pool, iam, networking, k8s-bootstrap)
  - envs/prod-us-west-2/ (layered stacks: network.tf, compute.tf, outputs.tf)
  - envs/staging-us-west-2/
- Module guidelines:
  - Modules must be versioned with tags (git tags + changelog).
  - Inputs/outputs must be minimal and well-documented.
  - Avoid provider alias proliferation; prefer single provider per region/account module.
- State management: remote state in encrypted S3 with DynamoDB locking (AWS) or GCS + Cloud KMS (GCP). State access limited to CI/CD service role and authorized engineers.

Terraform CI/CD pipeline (recommended pattern):
1. PR created against envs/* (requires at least two approvers for prod changes).
2. CI: terraform fmt, validate, static checks (tflint, checkov).
3. Plan stage: plan created and uploaded as artifact; human review required for changes to compute/gpu-node-pool modules.
4. Apply gating: for non-prod, merge triggers apply. For prod, apply executed by a scheduled, auditable approver (e.g., infra-deploy role via web UI).
5. Post-apply: run smoke tests (k8s node readiness, sample inference) and update capacity dashboard.

Safe change checklist (must be completed before applying changes that alter capacity/networking):
- Verified Terraform plan and diff; compute changes highlighted
- Change window scheduled (if removal/resize of nodes) and customer impact communicated
- Backups: snapshots of persistent disks created if modifying storage
- Rollback plan documented in PR description

Common CLI snippets / examples:
- Plan: terraform init && terraform plan -out=tfplan -var-file=secrets.tfvars
- Apply: terraform apply "tfplan"
- Drift detection: terraform plan -destroy -detailed-exitcode
- Assume role for target account (AWS): aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/infra-deploy --role-session-name tf-apply

CI/CD for k8s bootstrap and node pools:
- Provisioning sequence:
  1. Terraform creates VPC, subnets, security groups, and IAM roles.
  2. Terraform creates node pools (ASG / instance templates) with cloud-init that runs kubelet join scripts.
  3. Post-provision: bootstrap job registers nodes and taints applied for GPU workloads.
- Canary pattern: create a canary node pool with 1-2 nodes in target AZ and verify workload placement before scaling full pool.

Monitoring, alerts and dashboards (operational thresholds):
- Metrics to monitor: GPU utilization (per-model and per-node), pod OOMs, node CPU/Memory, pod startup latency, autoscaler queue length, instance failure rate, cloud quota usage.
- Alert examples:
  - alert_gpu_exhaustion: trigger when total free GPU slots < 10% for 10m -> SEV2
  - alert_node_provision_failures: > 3 failed provisioning ops in 5m -> SEV2
  - alert_autoscaler_stall: scaling decision pending > 10m with queue length > 3 -> SEV1
- Dashboards: per-region capacity heatmap, per-pool instance states, cost-per-GPU token estimate.

Runbook: common operational procedures
A) Scale-up (planned):
1. Open capacity change PR describing reason, regions, instance types, desired count.
2. Run terraform plan in CI and attach plan to PR.
3. After review, schedule a 30-minute change window and notify stake-holders.
4. Merge and apply via approved infra-deploy account.
5. Verify nodes become Ready in k8s, run smoke inference job, and confirm autoscaler behavior.
6. Update capacity dashboard and close change request.

B) Emergency scale-up (unexpected demand spike):
1. Triage: check dashboards, confirm spike source (customer vs test).
2. If short-term spike (< 2 hours), create on-demand node pool with faster instance type (if available) and set eviction policy for ephemeral workloads.
3. For persistent demand, follow standard PR + approval flow but mark high-priority with expedited approvals (infra lead + platform oncall).
4. If capacity cannot be provisioned due to quota, immediately open quota ticket with cloud provider and invoke temporary regional fallback (route traffic to secondary region).

C) Node failure / provisioning failure:
1. Identify failed nodes in cloud console and k8s.
2. If failure rate is isolated (<3 nodes), cordon + drain failed nodes, and rely on autoscaler to replace.
3. If failure rate impacts capacity significantly, scale up alternate pool and open incident.
4. Collect logs: cloud instance console logs, kubelet logs, system journal, and upload to incident channel.

D) Rollback procedure for a bad apply:
1. If apply created undesired capacity reduction, immediately reapply previous state from last successful state snapshot (use remote state backup).
2. For network/security regressions, revert the terraform commits and run plan/apply in staging first, then prod.
3. Communicate rollback and incident summary to stakeholders.

Maintenance windows and patching:
- Standard maintenance window: Sundays 02:00-06:00 UTC for non-critical regions.
- Minor patching (k8s patch, AMI refresh) can be batched and applied to canary pools first.
- Major changes (kernel upgrades, cluster upgrades) require 48-hour notice and a rollback plan.

Post-incident and runbook hygiene:
- After any SEV2/SEV1 incident involving capacity or networking, owner must open a postmortem within 72 hours, include timeline, root cause, remediation and action owner.
- Update this runbook with any procedural improvements and link the postmortem.

Appendix: sample terraform module interface (example)
- Module: modules/gpu-node-pool
  - inputs: ["instance_type", "desired_capacity", "max_capacity", "gpu_type", "spot_percentage", "ami_id"]
  - outputs: ["asg_name", "instance_profile", "node_group_id"]
